claims.text: Adjusting Al content in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni can induce localized short-range chemical ordering.
Atomic-size mismatch between Al and Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni causes the proposed localized ordering.
Electronic differences between Al and the other constituent elements cause the proposed localized ordering.
Al-induced short-range ordering lowers the local stacking-fault energy.
Lower local stacking-fault energy promotes nucleation of ordered L12 precipitates.
A limited Al-content window produces nanoscale ordered L12 precipitates embedded in a predominantly FCC matrix.
The L12 precipitates improve high-temperature strength by impeding dislocation motion.
The proposed microstructure also increases high-temperature strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
The nanoscale ordered precipitates act as sinks for radiation-induced defects.
Defect absorption by the precipitates improves radiation tolerance.
Retention of the FCC matrix sustains ductile deformation and twinning at cryogenic temperature.
Sustained FCC ductility and twinning improve cryogenic toughness relative to a lower-Al, disordered FCC baseline.
The L12-plus-FCC microstructure improves environmental resistance relative to the lower-Al baseline.
A lower-Al Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy remains a single-phase disordered FCC material.
The lower-Al disordered FCC baseline has lower high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic ductility.
Excessive Al promotes undesirable brittle intermetallic phases.
Too little Al fails to generate the short-range ordering required by the proposed mechanism.
AlxCrCoFeNi exhibits composition-dependent chemical clustering or short-range ordering over a range of temperatures.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis refers to near-equiatomic alloys while characterizing Al as present in 'small amounts,' whereas the initial state describes all five components as near-equiatomic. These descriptions imply materially different Al concentration regimes unless 'near-equiatomic' is defined more loosely.
